title: Logarithmic Embeddings into Probabilistic Spanning Trees for Distances and Capacities
summary: We prove that every connected $n$-vertex graph admits a probabilistic embedding into its spanning trees with expected distance stretch $O(\log n)$. This settles the logarithmic stretch conjecture of Alon, Karp, Peleg, and West, whose spanning-tree game appeared at the 1991 DIMACS Workshop on On-Line Algorithms and in SIAM Journal on Computing in 1995. A weighted form of the theorem also yields a distribution over spanning trees with capacities exactly equal to their fundamental graph cuts. Every tree dominates every graph cut, every cut is approximated within $O(\log n)$ in expectation, and the same capacity distribution defines an $O(\log n)$-competitive fractional oblivious routing. The distance and capacity distributions may differ. Diamond graphs give matching logarithmic lower bounds for stretch, congestion, and cut distortion. For rational input, both distributions are constructed deterministically in polynomial time and use at most $m$ trees, where $m$ is the number of graph edges. We prove an $\Omega(m/\rho)$ support lower bound for congestion $\rho$; in particular, $(1-o(1))m$ trees can be necessary for near-unit congestion, even when the optimum tends to one. Thus linear dependence on $m$ is unavoidable in this regime. The weighted theorem combines a protected-geodesic petal decomposition with a pathwise entropy bound for locally selected centers. A local averaging inequality derandomizes the radii, and an adaptive rational packing procedure constructs the distributions.

title: Beyond the Bochner Method: Optimal Spectral Gaps for Block Dynamics of Spin Systems like the $O(N)$ Model
summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on a spin system with $n$ sites and possibly infinite spin spaces. We prove local-to-global spectral-gap bounds for block Glauber dynamics. Given a symmetric, entrywise nonnegative matrix $A$ with zero diagonal and $\lambda_{\max}(A)<1$ encoding local spectral bounds for a spin system, we derive global spectral-gap bounds for block dynamics on its marginal distributions. These bounds are sharp: the Gaussian system with covariance $(I-A)^{-1}$ attains equality for every choice of disjoint blocks. Our proof extends the Bochner method through an abstract inequality for orthogonal projections on Hilbert spaces. As an application, we prove that Glauber dynamics for the $O(N)$ model, with $N\geq 2$, arbitrary external fields, and couplings of either sign, has spectral gap at least $(1-\|J_{\mathrm{abs}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}/N)/n$, where $J$ is the interaction matrix and $J_{\mathrm{abs}}=(|J_{ij}|)$. We also obtain spectral bounds for swap walks and local spectral expansion of partite simplicial complexes. For complexes formed from disjoint groups of ranks in random flags of subspaces over $\mathbb F_q$, we obtain a one-sided local spectral expansion bound of $2\sqrt q/(q+1)$. This bound is independent of the number and sizes of each group, and is nontrivial for every prime power $q$. Finally, for random forests $F$ of any finite graph with arbitrary positive edge weights, we prove that \[ \Pr(e,f\in F)\le \frac{4}{3} \Pr(e\in F)\Pr(f\in F) \] for distinct edges $e,f$, improving the factor 2 supplied by general log-concavity bounds for matroid independent sets. The argument combines our extended Bochner method with the analysis of an auxiliary real stable polynomial.

title: Santa Claus and Weighted Nash Social Welfare with Subadditive Valuations
summary: We study two fairness objectives for allocating $m$ indivisible items among $n$ agents with subadditive valuations: the max-min objective, also known as the Santa Claus problem, which maximizes the smallest value of an agent, and the weighted Nash social welfare, which maximizes the weighted geometric mean of the agents' values. For the max-min allocation problem, we give a randomized polynomial-time $O(\sqrt n)$-approximation algorithm for subadditive valuations with demand queries, improving the $2n-1$ bound of Khot and Ponnuswami. For additive valuations and for submodular valuations with value queries, we give simpler $O(\sqrt n)$-approximation algorithms. For additive valuations, this improves the $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ bound of Saha and Srinivasan. For these two classes, $O(m^\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms are also known for every constant $\varepsilon>0$. Our ratios depend only on $n$ and match, up to constants, the $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ integrality gap of the configuration LP. For the weighted Nash social welfare problem with subadditive valuations and demand queries, we give an $O(\Gamma(w))$-approximation algorithm, where $\Gamma(w)=\exp\bigl((\ln n-H(w))/2\bigr)$ and $H(w)$ is the entropy of the weight vector $w$. The factor $\Gamma(w)$ equals $1$ for equal weights and is at most $\sqrt n$ for all weights. We show that this ratio is tight for algorithms analyzed against the configuration LP: for every weight vector, the configuration LP has an integrality gap of $\Theta(\Gamma(w))$, even for XOS valuations, and this gap is $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ when one agent has almost all the weight. For submodular valuations, the configuration LP has a constant integrality gap for all weights.

title: Catalan Hashing: Efficient Linear Probing for Variable-Length Items
summary: A defining feature of the linear-probing hash table is its spatial locality: at load factor $1 - \varepsilon$, the hash table can be implemented so that each operation scans a single contiguous region of expected size $O(1/\varepsilon)$ (this is known as the \emph{scan cost}). This guarantee, however, relies on all items having unit size. In this paper, we ask whether it is possible to achieve a similar guarantee, but in a hash table that stores items of arbitrary lengths $|x| \ge 1$. title: Roundtrip All-Pairs Shortest Paths in Directed Graphs
summary: We study approximation algorithms for All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) in directed graphs under the roundtrip metric. In directed graphs, even finite-factor approximation of ordinary one-way distances must distinguish reachable from unreachable vertex pairs, and therefore computes transitive closure, a problem equivalent to Boolean matrix multiplication (BMM) under standard reductions. The roundtrip distance, defined as $\text{dist}_G(u \leftrightarrows v) = \text{dist}_G(u \to v) + \text{dist}_G(v \to u)$, offers a natural and robust relaxation. It measures the cost of traveling from $u$ to $v$ and back, satisfies the triangle inequality, and is inherently symmetric. While this metric has become central to the study of directed roundtrip spanners and compact routing, the fundamental problem of all-pairs roundtrip distance approximation has remained largely unexplored. In this work, we present a comprehensive study of roundtrip APSP and distance oracles, presenting several new lower and upper bounds. On the algorithmic side, our main result is a combinatorial algorithm that computes a stretch-$3$ approximation to all-pairs roundtrip distances in $\widetilde{O}(n^2 + \min\{m\sqrt{n},\, m^{1/3}n^{5/3}\})$ time. For edge weights in $[1,W]$, we also obtain a $(3+\varepsilon)$-approximation in $\widetilde O((n^{2.037}+nm^{2/3})\log(nW)/\varepsilon)$ time and a $(4+\varepsilon)$-approximation in $\widetilde O(n^{2.032}\log(nW)/\varepsilon)$ time using fast matrix multiplication. On the hardness side, we show that any stretch below $3$ would imply a breakthrough for BMM. We also obtain additional tradeoffs between stretch and running time.
